Using sideview with a screen reader

Source: vignettes/articles/screen-reader.Rmd
screen-reader.Rmd

sideview was first built as a visual canvas. Since 0.8.0 it also has a list view that reads top to bottom, and its checks print as plain sentences in the console. This page says how to use both.

How well is this tested

sideview 0.8.0 is checked with automated WCAG tests (axe) and real-browser keyboard tests; the NVDA script was run once in Edge with NVDA 2026.2 (all 15 tasks as written; the RStudio dialog and Viewer pane were not covered); not yet tested by blind users. Please treat it as a first step and tell us where it fails (see “Report a problem” below).

Start in the list view

The list view shows the same tables as text in one column. Start in it with the view argument or an option:

# for one call
sideview(patients, visits, view = "list")

# for the whole session
options(sideview.view = "list")

You can also press the List view button in the toolbar at any time. Switching is announced (“List view” or “Canvas view”) and focus moves to the first heading of the list.

The single-key shortcuts of the canvas (F, T, D and so on) can get in the way of a screen reader. They default to off in the list view. Turn them off everywhere with the “Keyboard shortcuts” switch in the ? list, or at the start with:

options(sideview.shortcuts = FALSE)

Ctrl+K and Ctrl+Enter always work.

A reading tour by headings

In the list view, move by headings (H in NVDA and JAWS, or the rotor in VoiceOver). The headings are:

  1. Summary: counts of tables, join steps and pipeline steps, whether code is ready, skip links, Save, Open and the keyboard shortcuts switch.
  2. Tables: one heading per table, for example “labs, 5,000 rows by 3 columns, full table.” Under it, one line per column (name, label, kind, and the distinct and missing counts) with Sort, Filter and Inspect buttons, then the rows as a captioned table, 25 a page, with Previous rows, Next rows and Go to row. A page change is announced (“Rows 26 to 50 of 5,000.”) and focus stays on the button.
  3. Join: pick two tables and their key columns, read the join check as sentences, and add the join.
  4. Merge SUPP: for a SUPP– table, check and add the merge into its parent.
  5. Transform: the step builders: Filter, Arrange, Mutate, Recode and Summarise.
  6. Pipeline: the steps so far, each of which you can switch off, move or delete.
  7. Code: the generated R code, with Copy (and Insert, in the gadget; a Shiny module has no Insert).
  8. Copilot: present only when a language model is set up.

What you do in the list view makes the same code as the canvas does, and a join made on the canvas shows in the list view’s Pipeline.

Results as sentences in the console

The results of the checks print as sentences, not as lists of numbers. For example:

chk <- sv_join_diagnostics(patients, visits, by = "patient_id")
chk                       # "Join of patients and visits by patient_id is one to many. ..."

sv_column_profile(patients, "age")
sv_supp_check(ae, suppae)
sv_detect_discrepancies(patients, "sex")
sv_suggest_mappings(patients, visits)

unclass(chk)              # the raw list, if you want the numbers

sv_describe() writes one sentence for each table and one line for each column. It is the text twin of looking at the cards:

patients <- data.frame(
  id  = 1:6,
  sex = c("M", "F", "F", NA, "M", "F"),
  age = c(40, 51, 62, 38, 45, 29)
)
sv_describe(patients)

A large duckdb or Arrow table is described from its summaries and is never loaded into memory.

Keyboard and low vision

If you can see the screen, at least in part, or cannot use a mouse, you can use the canvas itself. Turn on the Accessible canvas switch: press ? and use the switch in the dialog, or start with it on.

# for one call
sideview(patients, visits, access = TRUE)

# for the whole session
options(sideview.access = TRUE)

The argument or option only sets the starting state. The switch in the ? dialog changes it, and the browser remembers that choice, which wins over R. With the switch off the canvas is unchanged.

With the switch on:

  • The zoom never goes below 100%. Text is at least 16 px, every control is at least 24 by 24 px, the focus ring is 3 px, and a high-contrast colour set replaces the theme colours. Joins are 3 px wide with a dash pattern and an arrowhead each, so crossing joins can be told apart without colour.
  • Each card is one Tab stop, in reading order. On a card, Arrows move it 20 px (Shift+Arrows 100 px), Alt+Arrows focus the nearest card, Enter goes to its first column header, and PageUp, PageDown, Home and End scroll its table. The view follows focus.
  • On a column header, Left and Right move along the columns and Esc goes back to the card. C starts a join and Enter completes it on the column you have moved to (Esc cancels), Delete removes a join (a small menu if there are several), and J jumps to the joined column. Moves and joins are announced. The keys work with the single-key shortcuts off and never fire while you type.
  • Windows High Contrast and “increase contrast” are followed even with the switch off.

Alt+Left is also the browser’s Back key. sideview cancels it for the jump, but this has not yet been checked in Edge or in RStudio. If it takes you back in your setup, the list view still gives you every join and filter by keyboard, and please report it.

Use a browser, not the RStudio pane

For a screen reader we recommend the gadget in a real browser:

sideview(patients, visits, viewer = "browser", view = "list")

The reason is what the tests can and cannot show. The keyboard and axe tests run in a real browser, where the page has full keyboard and assistive-technology support. How the RStudio Viewer pane and the RStudio dialog pass keys and speech to a screen reader has not been measured: we have not yet read them with a screen reader, so we make no claim about them. Until that is done, use viewer = "browser". The saved HTML widget (save_sideview()) opens in a browser too.

Report a problem

If something is not read, is read wrongly or cannot be reached by keyboard, please open an accessibility issue. Tell us your screen reader and its version, the browser or RStudio pane, what you did and what you heard.
